TENTATIVE RULING(S) FOR March 6, 2026
Department S14 – Judge Winston Keh
This court follows California Rules of Court, rule 3.1308(b) for tentative rulings. (See San
Bernardino Superior Court Local Emergency Rule 8.) Tentative rulings for each law & motion
will be posted on the internet (https://www.sb-court.org) by 3:00 p.m. on the court day
immediately before the hearing.
You may appear in person at the hearing although remote appearance by CourtCall is preferred.
(See www.sb-court.org/general-information/remote-access ).
If you do not have Internet access or if you experience difficulty with the posted tentative ruling,
you may obtain the tentative ruling by calling the department (S-14) at (909) 521-3495 or the
Administrative Assistant (909) 708-8756, who prepared the ruling.
If you (or both parties) wish to submit on the Tentative, notify the other party and call the
department by 4:00 pm the day before and your appearance may be excused unless the
Court orders you to appear.
You must appear at the hearing if you are so directed by the court in the tentative ruling. Be
prepared to address those issues set forth by the court in its ruling.
UNLESS OTHERWISE NOTED, THE PREVAILING PARTY IS TO GIVE NOTICE OF THE
RULING.
CIVSB2425104
Cisneros v. City of Hesperia
__________________________________________________________________________
TENTATIVE RULING(S):
Before the Court is the City’s Motion for Summary Judgment, or in the alternative summary
adjudication, on the grounds that Cisneros cannot show that the harassment was severe or
pervasive; the retaliation claim fails because Cisneros cannot show a legally cognizable adverse
employment action; there were legitimate business reasons for any adverse employment action;
Cisneros cannot show a causal connection between any allegedly protected activity and any
adverse employment action; and Cisneros cannot show that he engaged in activity protected
under the Labor Code.
The motion is supported by a separate statement of fact; declarations from Rita Perez (the City’s
Deputy HR Director), Rachel Molina (the City Manager), and Alison Kalinski (defense counsel);
portions of the transcript from the deposition of Cisneros; text messages from Meaden; excerpts
from a text message log; a shelter dog Facebook post; the social media radio post; a “timeline”;
a staff memorandum regarding staff council relations; a notice of intent to terminate Cisneros
with attachments; e-mails between Cisneros and Caleb Enriquez (an eventual supervisor of
Cisneros); and administrative leave with pay document; a notice of internal administrative
investigation; a resignation e-mail from Cisneros; and another e-mail from Cisneros to Jessica
Perry.
The opposition is supported by an opposing separate statement of fact, evidentiary objections, a
declaration from Cisneros, a declaration from Tamarin Peeden (an administrative assistant), a
declaration from attorney Vasili Brasinikas, an e-mail regarding injured dogs, Cisneros’s notes
about “inhumane and illegal directives,” e-mail chains between Cisneros and Enriquez, a training
memorandum, an administrative leave letter, a notice of completion of investigation, a notice of
intent to terminate, a resignation letter, and portions of the transcript from Cisneros’s and
councilmember Cameron Gregg’s deposition.
In connection with the reply, the City also submits evidentiary objections.
ANALYSIS
The First Cause of Action for Harassment and Issue No. 1
To prevail on a claim for harassment against an employer, the plaintiff must plead and prove (1)
he was an employee of or providing services under a contract with the defendant, (2) he was
subjected to unwanted harassing conduct because of his protected status, (3) the harassing
conduct was severe or pervasive, (4) a reasonable person in the plaintiff’s circumstances would
have considered the work environment to be hostile or abusive, (5) the plaintiff considered the
work environment to be hostile or abusive, (6) the supervisor engaged in the conduct or the
defendant knew or should have known of the conduct and failed to take immediate and
appropriate corrective action, and (7) the conduct was a substantial factor in causing plaintiff’s
harm. (CACI 2521A and Government Code § 12940, subd. (j)(1).)
“An employer is not liable for nonsupervisor, coworker harassment if it takes prompt, reasonable
and efficacious remedial action. ([Government Code] § 12940, subd. (j)(1) [harassment of an
employee or applicant by an employee other than an agent or supervisor shall be unlawful if the
entity, or its agents or supervisors, knows or should have known of this conduct and fails to take
immediate and appropriate corrective action].” (Mathieu v. Norrell Corp. (2004) 115 Cal.App.4th
1174, 1184; Rehmani v. Superior Court (2012) 204 Cal.App.4th 945, 952 [“When the harasser is
a nonsupervisory employee, employer liability turns on a showing of negligence”].)
Furthermore, “simple teasing, offhand comments, and isolated incidents (unless extremely
serious) will not amount to discriminatory changes in the terms and conditions of employment.”
(Faragher v. City of Boca Raton (1998) 524 U.S. 775, 788.) In short, FEHA is not a civility code
and is not designed to rid the workplace of vulgarity. (Lyle v. Warner Bros. Television
Productions (2006) 38 Cal.4th 295.)
However, effective January 2019, Government Code section 12923 provides “harassment
creates a hostile, offensive, oppressive, or intimidating work environment and deprives victims of
their statutory right to work in a place free of discrimination when the harassing conduct
sufficiently offends, humiliates, distresses, or intrudes upon its victim, so as to disrupt the victim’s
emotional tranquility in the workplace, affect the victim’s ability to perform the job as usual, or
otherwise interfere with and undermine the victim’s personal sense of well-being.”
The statute further indicates, at subdivision (a), “the plaintiff need not prove that his or her
tangible productivity has declined as a result of the harassment. It suffices to prove that a
reasonable person subjected to the discriminatory conduct would find, as the plaintiff did, that
the harassment so altered working conditions as to make it more difficult to do the job.” The
statute further provides “[a] single incident of harassing conduct is sufficient to create a triable
issue regarding the existence of a hostile work environment if the harassing conduct has
unreasonably interfered with the plaintiff’s work performance or created an intimidating, hostile,
or offensive working environment.” Finally, subdivision (e) of the statute indicates “[h]arassment
cases are rarely appropriate for disposition on summary judgment. In that regard, the Legislature
affirms the decision in Nazir v. United Airlines, Inc. (2009) 178 Cal.App.4th 243 and its
observation that hostile working environment cases involve issues ‘not determinable on paper.’”
Whether, objectively, the misconduct can be seen as severe or pervasive
In this case, the City has not attempted to disprove the fact that Cisneros was called “Juanathan”
about 15 times each by five individuals and via text message by Meaden; that he was called
“Juanie” about five times; nor does the City refute the proposition that a dog was named and
advertised as “Juanathan” via multiple mediums. The evidence also supports the proposition that
the dogs were commonly named after employees. Meaden, a supervisor, was also involved,
sent the text message, and even introduced Cisneros to co-workers as Juanathan. (Fact No.’s 1,
3-4, 10, 15-16, 18, 80-82, 87; Cisneros Dep. at p. 29, 31, and 36; Peeden Decl. at ¶¶ 5 and 7.)
The City nevertheless argues that the name-calling does not amount to severe or pervasive
conduct, but as the legislature has noted, even a single incident of harassing conduct may be
sufficient to create a triable issue regarding the existence of a hostile work environment, and the
issue is generally not appropriately resolved via summary judgment. The California Supreme
Court has also recently made clear that “a single racial epithet can be so offensive it gives rise to
a triable issue of actionable harassment.” (Bailey v. San Francisco Dist. Attorney's Office (2024)
16 Cal.5th 611, 629 [addressing the “N” word]; see also Boyer-Liberto v. Fontainebleau Corp.
(4th Cir. 2015) 786 F.3d 264, 280 [reasonable jury could find “two uses of the ‘porch monkey’
epithet—whether viewed as a single incident or as a pair of discrete instances of harassment—
were severe enough to engender a hostile work environment].)
The Supreme Court further explained that “[r]acially motivated comments or actions may appear
innocent or only mildly offensive to one who is not a member of the targeted group,” but
“intolerably abusive or threatening when understood from the perspective of a plaintiff who is a
member of the targeted group.” (Bailey v. San Francisco Dist. Attorney's Office (2024) 16 Cal.5th
611, 629.) The allegations of racial hostility therefore must be considered “from the perspective
of a reasonable person belonging to the racial or ethnic group of the plaintiff.” (Ibid.)
Furthermore, the status of the speaker, such as the words from a supervisor versus a coworker,
may be a “significant factor” in “assessing the severity of harassing conduct” and the less severe
the word, the more pervasive its use generally must be and vice versa. (Id. at pp. 629-630 and
633.)
While, here, the term “Juanathan” and “Juanie” are not as severe as the “N” word, the City
appears to concede that the term could be construed as racially derogatory. The City otherwise
produces no evidence undermining that proposition, and, to the contrary, the investigative report
submitted shows that at least the City’s own investigator concluded the term was “derogatory.”
(See City’s Ex. 9 at Bates Stamp p. 144; Opening Brief at p. 30 [suggesting the term amounts to
“simple teasing” and that no “other raced-based” conduct occurred, thus indicating the
nicknames could be construed as race-based].) Indeed, the term could be seen as disrespectful
to Cisneros and his formal first name (Johnathan) and it appears to be a potentially mocking
mashup between Cisneros’ first name and the traditional Hispanic counterpart “Juan” as
opposed to “Jonatán,” thus giving the nickname racial undertones.
Furthermore, while the term is not as bad as the “N” word, it was used by at least five coworkers
around 15 times each within a year’s time, it was used to introduce Cisneros to others, it was
used during Cisneros’ probationary period, the supervisor Meaden texted Cisneros about the
nickname and she introduced him to coworkers using that name, and a dog was named and
advertised using the same name, apparently being named after Cisneros. Thus, it cannot be
said, as a matter of law, that no reasonable person in the Cisneros’s circumstances would have
considered the work environment to be hostile or abusive.
The City also suggests that Cisneros himself never considered the work environment to be
hostile or abusive, i.e., the incidents were not subjectively offensive. The evidence supports the
proposition that Cisneros never complained, never stated it bothered him, and that he never
asked anyone not to call him Juanathan. While Cisneros now states in his declaration that he
complained to some coworkers, those assertions conflict with the testimony he gave during his
deposition and should therefore be disregarded under the D’Amico rule. (Compare Cisneros
Decl. at ¶¶ 5-6 with City’s Ex. 1 [Dep. Transcript] at pp. 33-35; Fact No.’s 10-13.) Indeed,
Cisneros even seemed to jokingly welcome the name in response to the text message from
Meaden. (Fact No. 8.)
Nevertheless, Cisneros declares that the name was demoralizing to the work environment, it was
offensive and bothersome, and he perceived it as racist (Cisneros Decl. at ¶¶ 5-9.) Thus, while
the lack of complaints could show that Cisneros was not subjectively bothered by the names, his
declaration now creates a triable issue of material fact on the issue. The Court also at this point
cannot weight the evidence and Cisneros provides a valid explanation for why he did not “speak
up,” namely, because he was on probation and feared losing his job. (Cisneros Decl. at ¶ 5.) As
noted, the name calling also appears to have started with Cisneros’s supervisor, or at least she
perpetuated it via the co-workers.
Since the City has not met its initial burden of disproving the severe and pervasive argument and
since there is a triable issue of material fact as to whether Cisneros subjectively considered the
environment hostile, the motion is denied as to the first cause of action for harassment and issue
no. 1. Since the claim is also viable based upon the name calling alone, the Court need not
address the other potential grounds for the harassment claim. (See Notice of Motion at 2:15-22
[motion based on the argument that the cause of action, as a whole, is invalid].)
The Second Cause of Action for Retaliation under FEHA and Issue No.’s 2-4
“[I]n order to establish a prima facie case of retaliation under the FEHA, a plaintiff must show (1)
he or she engaged in a ‘protected activity,’ (2) the employer subjected the employee to an
adverse employment action, and (3) a causal link existed between the protected activity and the
employer’s action.” (Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1042.)
An employee “need not formally file a charge in order to qualify as being engaged in protected
opposing activity,” but “complaints about personal grievances or vague or conclusory remarks
that fail to put an employer on notice as to what conduct it should investigate will not suffice to
establish protected conduct.” (Glynn v. Superior Court (2019) 42 Cal.App.5th 47, 55 [involving a
FEHA retaliation claim].) ‘The relevant question ... is not whether a formal accusation of
discrimination is made but whether the employee’s communications to the employer sufficiently
convey the employee’s reasonable concerns that the employer has acted or is acting in an
unlawful discriminatory manner.’” (Ibid.)
Furthermore, FEHA retaliation must be based upon retaliation for activity protected under FEHA.
(Nejadian v. County of Los Angeles (2019) 40 Cal.App.5th 703, 722 [“Government Code section
12940, subdivision (h) makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to retaliate
against an employee because that employee opposed any practice forbidden by FEHA or
because the employee filed a complaint, testified, or assisted in any proceeding under FEHA”].)
In this case, the claimed protected activity is the alleged opposition of the unlawful harassment,
which as noted above is prohibited under FEHA. (FAC at ¶ 30.) It is also undisputed that on July
11, 2023, and in response to an e-mail from Caleb Enriquez, Cisneros alleged he was being
subjected to a hostile work environment. (Fact No.’s 34-35.)
In particular, Enriquez became the acting Code Compliance Manager and Cisneros’s supervisor
on June 19, 2023, and acted as his supervisor for about 18 days, or until Cisneros was placed
on administrative leave on July 14, 2023. (Fact No.’s 25-26.) Enriques was purportedly rude to,
and demeaned, Cisneros during two meetings, essentially cutting him off as he was attempting
to ask a question during a meeting. Cisneros was told not to ask further questions or write them
down to e-mail later. (Fact No.’s 27-30; see also Fact No.’s 31-35 [addressing the substance of
the subsequent e-mails].) The issue was then addressed via e-mail, at which time Cisneros
broadly complained about a hostile work environment. A private investigator was then retained to
investigate the claim on July 13, 2023. (Fact No. 36.) Cisneros was placed on leave on July 14,
2023, or just a few days after the e-mail complaint. (Fact No. 92.)
The adverse employment action element
In the motion, the City argues Cisneros did not suffer an adverse employment action in the few
days between the complaint and the leave and that the leave itself does not constitute an
adverse employment action. An adverse employment action is one that materially affects the
terms, conditions, or privileges of employment or treatment that would deter an employee from
engaging in protective activity. (McRae v. Dep’t of Corr. & Rehab (2006) 142 Cal.App.4th 377,
386; see also CACI 2509 [“adverse employment action” explained].)
Cisneros’ limited interactions with Enriquez, in the short limited time period at-issue, does not
constitute an adverse employment action. (See Fact No.’s 95-97 and 151-155.) However, there
is authority indicating that leave, even paid administrative leave, can constitute an adverse
employment action. (See Horsford v. Board of Trustees of California State University (2005) 132
Cal.App.4th 359, 374 [“in the particular factual context of employment as a peace officer,
suspension from duty for lying on a police report … even if the leave is with pay, constitutes
adverse employment action” as the “charge can destroy a police officer’s career”]; see also
Whitehall v. County of San Bernardino (2017) 17 Cal.App.5th 352, 367 [leave which was not
requested and which was not intended as a reward or accommodation, but which was required
to investigate the plaintiff’s own wrongdoing, can constitute an adverse employment action even
if the plaintiff remains on payroll].) Federal cases similarly hold that leave can constitute an
adverse employment action (Ibid. [collecting cases].)
In this case, while the leave was paid (Fact No. 101), it was not requested by Cisneros nor was it
a reward. Instead, the leave was to purportedly investigate if Cisneros illegally recorded a
coworker. (See, e.g., Fact No.’s 93, 103, 105-106, 110-111, and 117.) However, it is undisputed
that truthfulness, integrity, and professionalism are important traits for an animal control officer
(Fact No. 115) and in that regard Cisneros’s position was not too dissimilar to the peace office in
Horsford, supra. Consequently, the leave, if retaliatory and pretext as alleged, could have
destroyed Cisneros’s career. Thus, it cannot be said under the circumstances that the
administrative leave cannot constitute an adverse employment action.
The City’s legitimate basis for the leave
“California has adopted the three-stage burden-shifting test established by the United States
Supreme Court for trying claims of discrimination ... based on a theory of disparate treatment”
because “such claims must usually be proved circumstantially.” (Department of Fair Employment
and Housing v. Lucent Technologies, Inc. (9th Cir. 2011) 642 F.3d 728, 745 (internal cites to
California precedent omitted).) Notably, the same analyses apply to discrimination and retaliation
claims. (Guz v. Bechtel Nat. Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 362 (Guz).)
“Generally, the plaintiff [has] an initial burden of establishing a prima facie case of discrimination.
When an employer moves for summary judgment, however, the burden is reversed ... because
the defendant who seeks summary judgment bears the initial burden. Thus, [t]o prevail on
summary judgment, [the employer is] required to show either that (1) plaintiff could not establish
one of the elements of [the] FEHA claim or (2) there was a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason
for its decision to terminate plaintiff’s employment.” (Department of Fair Employment and
Housing v. Lucent Technologies, Inc. (9th Cir. 2011) 642 F.3d 728, 745 (internal cites to
California precedent omitted).)
If the employer meets its burden, the burden then shifts back to the plaintiff to demonstrate that
the employer’s alleged reason for the adverse employment decision is a pretext for another
motive which is retaliatory or discriminatory. (Guz, supra, 24 Cal.4th 317, 354-56; Akers v.
County of San Diego (2002) 95 Cal.App.4th 1441, 1453.) Pretext can be shown by inference
from the timing of the discharge, the identity of the decision maker, or by the discharged
employee’s job performance before termination. (Hanson v. Lucky Stores, Inc. (1999) 74
Cal.App.4th 215, 224.) The plaintiff must raise an issue as to the employer’s credibility with facts
demonstrating weaknesses, implausibilities, inconsistencies, incoherence, or contradictions in
the employer’s proffered legitimate reason so a factfinder could rationally find them unworthy of
credence. (Cucuzza v. City of Santa Clara (2002) 104 Cal.App.4th 1031, 1038.) It is insufficient
to show the employer’s decision was wrong, mistaken, or unwise. (Horn v. Cushman &
Wakefield Western (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 798, 807.)
To avoid summary judgment, the employee must produce “substantial responsive
evidence” that the employer’s proffered explanation was untrue or pretextual. (University of
Southern California v. Superior Court (1990) 222 Cal.App.3d 1028, 1039.) On the other hand, at
the summary judgment stage, the plaintiff need not prove that the employer’s explanation for its
acts was untrue; he need only present sufficient evidence to support an inference that the
employer’s motive was discriminatory or retaliatory. (Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24
Cal.4th 317, 360-361.)
In this case, it is undisputed that Cisneros recorded Enriquez without his consent and
gave the recording to Gregg. (Fact No.’s 103 and 112.) Gregg in turn provided the recording the
City Manager, Rachel Molina, who watched the video and believed it was recorded without
Enriquez’s consent. Since Cisneros was responsible for issuing citations as part of his job,
Molina believed that a potential criminal conviction of Cisneros would undermine his credibility
and integrity. Thus, the City contends that is why Cisneros was placed on administrative leave.
(Molina Decl. at pp. 4-5; Fact No.’s 110.)
Since the basis for the leave has been shown to be legitimate, the burden shifts to
Cisneros to show pretext. While Cisneros argues that when a stated reason for an adverse
employment action is false that it can be a sign of unlawful motive (Opposition at 20:18-12), it is
notable that in this case Cisneros concedes he recorded the conversation without Enriquez’s
without his consent. Cisneros also admitted that such conduct is illegal. (Fact No. 116.) As noted
above, Cisneros further agrees that truthfulness, integrity, and professionalism are important
traits of an animal control officer. (Fact No. 115.) Cisneros additionally admitted during his
deposition that he was placed on leave because he recorded the conversation without consent
(Fact No. 117 and Cisneros’ Dep. at p. 106), though the underlying testimony could be construed
as a concession as to what he was told about the leave not the veracity of the reason.
Cisneros also notes the timing of the leave in comparison to the complaints. In the
retaliation context, the “close proximity in time of an adverse action to an employee’s resistance
or opposition to unlawful conduct is often strong evidence of a retaliatory motive.” (Scotch v. Art
Institute of California (2009) 173 Cal.App.4th 986, 1020.) However, “temporal proximity alone is
not sufficient to create a triable issue as to pretext,” that is once the burden has shifted to the
plaintiff under the McDonnel Douglas test. (Arteaga v. Brink’s, Inc. (2008) 163 Cal.App.4th 327,
341.)
The only other issue raised by Cisneros is an interaction on June 13, 2023, during which
Meaden purportedly, following a union meeting, directed staff not to communicate with Cisneros
and to report any interactions. (See Opposition at p. 21 and Response to Fact No. 93 [citing
Cisneros Decl. at ¶ 22].) The conduct, however, predates the report of harassment and appears
more directed at the claims related to the animal welfare, as opposed to the claim of harassment
which came later, so it is unclear why it would show pretext.
Overall, the City showed a legitimate basis for the paid leave (the secret recording) and
Cisneros failed to produce substantial evidence of pretext and admits to the basis for the
investigation. Additionally, based on his concessions to the investigator about his misconduct
(Fact No. 112) the City’s investigator also concluded Cisneros recorded Enriques without
consent. (Fact No. 114.) It was then under that threat of termination that Cisneros resigned.
(Additional Fact No. 315.) Thus, to the extent Cisneros quit based on a substantiated claim for
misconduct, misconduct he admits to, he also cannot advance a viable claim for constructive
discharge.
The Third Cause of Action for Retaliation under the Labor Code
Labor Code section 1102.5 provides “whistleblower protections to employees who disclose
wrongdoing to authorities. As relevant here, section 1102.5 prohibits an employer from retaliating
against an employee for sharing information the employee “has reasonable cause to believe ...
discloses a violation of state or federal statute” or of “a local, state, or federal rule or regulation”
with a government agency, with a person with authority over the employee, or with another
employee who has authority to investigate or correct the violation. (§ 1102.5, subd. (b).) “This
provision … reflects the broad public policy interest in encouraging workplace whistle-blowers to
report unlawful acts without fearing retaliation.” (Lawson v. PPG Architectural Finishes, Inc.
(2022) 12 Cal.5th 703, 709.)
The protected activity element: Issue no. 5
The City first argues that Cisneros did not engage in protected activity since he does not recall
whether he shared his concerns about violations of “animal laws” with anyone but Gregg. (Fact
No. 172.) The evidence cited, however, indicates Cisneros was asked whether he shared his
concerns with anyone “outside the city.” (Cisneros Dep. at pp. 258.) The evidence therefore
does not support the proposition asserted. It is also notable that subdivision (e) of Labor Code
section 1102.5 indicates that a report “made by an employee of a government agency to their
employer is a disclosure of information to a government or law enforcement agency” for
purposes of the statute. The City does not argue that the complaint to Gregg would not qualify
for protection under section 1102.5 based on who the recipient was.
Instead, the City suggests that the complaint was not protected based on its contents. The City
indicates Cisneros does not recall that he told Gregg anything besides the fact that animals were
in dirty cages and there was a dog with a broken leg. (Fact No. 173.) To the extent the City
suggests that Cisneros’s inability to recall shifts the burden, “[p]ointing out the absence of
evidence to support a plaintiff’s claim is insufficient to meet the moving defendant’s initial burden
of production. The defendant must also produce evidence that the plaintiff cannot reasonably
obtain evidence to support his or her claim.” (Gaggero v. Yura (2003) 108 Cal.App.4th 884, 891.)
In any event, the City notes that Gregg further alleges he told Gregg the animals were left in
“horrible medical conditions and not being treated,” which violated “animal law.” (Fact No. 164.)
The City then suggests that Cisneros has failed to identify what law was violated and his
reference to “animal law” is insufficient. However, it is not clear if the City asked Cisneros, via
written discovery, what law was purportedly violated. His inability to cite a specific law during the
deposition is also not necessarily dispositive. (See Rifkind v. Sup.Ct. (Good) (1994) 22
Cal.App.4th at 1262-1263 [“law-to-fact application” is “beyond the competence of most lay
persons” and “[t]here is no legitimate reason to put the deponent to that exercise … This is what
lawyers are for”].)
In general terms, it would be reasonable to suspect that neglect of an animal is illegal, and that is
essentially what Cisneros complained about. The disclosure also did not have to actually involve
a violation of the law, rather there simply must have been “reasonable cause to believe” the
report “discloses a violation of state or federal statute.” The opposition also cites to Penal Code
section 597, which makes animal cruelty unlawful and covers “needless suffering” of animals not
just intentional or malicious actions as the reply suggests. Again, it is important to note that the
misconduct alleged did not actually have to constitute a crime as instead the complaint is
protected if there was a reasonable belief. Overall, the motion is denied as to Issue No. 5.
The adverse employment action: Issue No. 6
The City next argues that Cisneros did not suffer an adverse employment action, but as noted
above the paid administrative leave can qualify as an adverse employment action.
The causal link element and the “same actions” defense: Issue no.’s 7-8
Finally, the City essentially adopts the same argument advanced in connection with the FEHA
claim and notes that it had a legitimate basis for placing Cisneros on leave; it would have done
so regardless of whether Cisneros made the complaint; and there is no causal link between the
complaint and the leave.
However, Labor Code “section 1102.6, and not McDonnell Douglas, supplies the applicable
framework for litigating and adjudicating section 1102.5 whistleblower claims. By its terms,
section 1102.6 describes the applicable substantive standards and burdens of proof for both
parties in a section 1102.5 retaliation case: First, it must be “demonstrated by a preponderance
of the evidence” that the employee’s protected whistleblowing was a “contributing factor” to an
adverse employment action. (§ 1102.6.) Then, once the employee has made that necessary
threshold showing, the employer bears “the burden of proof to demonstrate by clear and
convincing evidence” that the alleged adverse employment action would have occurred “for
legitimate, independent reasons” even if the employee had not engaged in protected
whistleblowing activities.” ” (Lawson v. PPG Architectural Finishes, Inc. (2022) 12 Cal.5th 703,
712.)
Therefore, under section 1102.6, the plaintiff “does not need to show that the employer’s
nonretaliatory reason was pretextual. Even if the employer had a genuine, nonretaliatory reason
for its adverse action, the plaintiff still carries the burden assigned by statute if it is shown that
the employer also had at least one retaliatory reason that was a contributing factor in the action.”
(Lawson v. PPG Architectural Finishes, Inc. (2022) 12 Cal.5th 703, 715-716.) Summary
judgment, however, is still potentially possible. (Ibid. [citing Texas v. Lesage (1999) 528 U.S. 18,
20 and 21—upholding a grant of summary judgment and noting the government “can avoid
liability by proving that it would have made the same decision without the impermissible
motive”].)
“To satisfy the “clear and convincing” burden of proof under California law, the evidence must be
“so clear as to leave no substantial doubt,” and “sufficiently strong to command the unhesitating
assent of every reasonable mind.” (Lawson v. PPG Architectural Finishes, Inc. (9th Cir., July 2,
2024, No. 22-56114) 2024 WL 3272932, at *1.) The employer “does not satisfy its burden just by
demonstrating that it had a legitimate reason to take the challenged employment action” as it
must also demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence “it would have” terminated the
employment event if the employee “not engaged in protected activity.” (Id. at p. 2-3.)
The differing framework is significant in this case because temporal proximity can establish a
causal connection between the protected activity and the adverse employment action, even if it
does not constitute “substantial evidence” for purpose of showing pretext under McDonnell
Douglas. (Arteaga v. Brink's, Inc. (2008) 163 Cal.App.4th 327, 353 [“temporal proximity between
an employee’s disclosure … and a subsequent termination may satisfy the causation
requirement at the first step of the burden-shifting process,” but it alone “is not sufficient to raise
a triable issue as to pretext once the employer has offered evidence of a legitimate,
nondiscriminatory reason for the termination”].)
Under Lawson though, Cisneros need not show pretext, but he has shown a causal connection.
The City must therefore meet the heavier burden of clear and convincing evidence in the face of
temporal proximity between the protected activity and the leave, which can be considered, and it
must do so under the heavier clear and convincing standard. (See Fact No. 173 [discussion with
Gregg occurred on June 30, 2023] and Fact No. 198[Cisneros placed on leave on July 14,
2023].) It is also notable that the City did not review the evidence that Cisneros provided, albeit
illegally obtained, until much closer to the leave date. (See Fact No. 103.) Thus, timing of the
receipt and review of the recording in relation to the leave could plausibly show retaliation as
well, at least to the extent the City knew Cisneros had evidence to back his claim.
Overall, there is a triable issue of material fact as to whether the leave was retaliatory given the
temporal proximity and the applicable standard of review. The motion is therefore denied as to
the third cause of action and issue no.’s 7-8. While not raised by Cisneros, it is also notable
Labor Code section 98.6 provides that “[i]f an employer engages in any action prohibited by this
section within 90 days of the protected activity specified in this section, there shall be a
rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee’s claim.” The statute makes it illegal to retaliate
“because the employee or applicant engaged in any conduct delineated in this chapter … and
Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 1101) of Part 3 of Division 2.” (Lab. Code, § 98.6.) Labor
Code section 1102.5 is found within Chapter 5 of Part 3 of Division 2 of the Labor Code. Thus,
the implication is that the presumption would apply in this case.
RULING
For all the reasons set forth above, the Court rules as follows:
(1) The Court overrules Cisneros’s three evidentiary objections.
a. If nothing else the evidence is relevant and admissible to show state of mind, which
relates to Cisneros’s claim that the adverse employment action was illegally
motivated.
(2) The Court overrules, as to the Cisneros declaration, the City’s objection no.’s 1, 2, 5, 6, 7
(except as to the latter portion), 9, 10, 11, 12 (as to Cisneros not being invited), 14, 16-22,
24, 26-34, 38, 40, 45, 48, 50, and 51; sustains objection no.’s 8, 13, 15, 23, 36, 37, 43, 44,
46, 47, and 49 on foundational or hearsay grounds; and sustains objection no.’s 35, 39, and
41-42 (as to the actual contents) on best evidence grounds. While objection no.’s 3-4 are not
true evidentiary objections, the Court notes the D’Amico rule applies. The Court overrules
objection no.’s 1, 2-4, 6, and 7, but sustains objection no. 5 on foundational or hearsay
grounds as to the Peeden declaration. The Court sustains the objection to exhibit 1 but
overrules as to exhibit 2. As to exhibit 10, overrules objection no.’s 1-3 and 6-8, but sustains
as to objection no.’s 4-5 and 9-12. Finally, as to exhibit 12, sustains objection no.’s 1-3 and 5,
but overrules objection no.’s 4 and 6.
a. At times the evidence may not be admissible to prove the truth of the matters
asserted, but to show Cisneros’ subjective beliefs about the harassment, the
perceived law violations, and the reasonableness of the beliefs, whether reports were
made, and whether he was offended by the alleged harassment. It is also notable that
many of the objections are overbroad, which is improper and grounds for overruling
the objections. (OCFCD v. Sunny Crest Dairy, Inc. (1978) 77 Cal. App. 3d 742, 753.)
(3) The Court Denies the motion for summary judgment.
(4) The Court Denies the motion for summary adjudication as to the first cause of action and
issue no. 1.
(5) The Court Grants the motion for summary adjudication as to the second cause of action and
issue no. 3 (rendering the remaining issues moot).
(6) The Court Denies the motion for summary adjudication as to the third cause of action and
issue no.’s 5-8.
